game.summary:
Built the §17 walking skeleton as npm workspaces: apps/web (Phaser client with landing page, HUD, keyboard adapter, input sender, snapshot interpolation), apps/server (Colyseus MatchRoom: one room per private match, filterBy code, static onAuth refusing protocol mismatch/unknown code/full match, 60 Hz setFixedTimestep with world logic every third step, Schema mirror patched at 20 Hz, InputGate dropping malformed/oversized/stale/future-frame/over-rate input), packages/simulation (integer fixed-point state, seeded mulberry32 in state, spawn slots, hashState = FNV-1a 64 over canonical JSON), packages/protocol (version, zod join/input schemas, validation), packages/content (sea map, spawn slots, ship speed, slice/alpha presets, §8 frame budgets with validators), packages/test-tools (HeadlessClient on @colyseus/sdk). Added README.md, docs/architecture.md, the CLAUDE.md commands line, and READMEs for assets/source, assets/exported and infra. Checks I ran: I copied the tree to a fresh directory and ran npm ci with an empty cache, then all five policy checks there. typecheck passed, test:unit passed (70 tests), test:integration passed (8 tests), build passed, and the Playwright browser run with --reporter=json --workers=1 --retries=0 CI=1 passed 2 of 2. check-report --all accepted both scenarios. In the worktree I also ran integration three more times and the browser spec twice more; all passed. Nothing is committed: the task forbids commits.

Operator repair 1: The verifier parses only unittest or Node TAP/spec summaries; Vitest's summary gave no test evidence, so a reporter now prints Vitest's counts in the Node summary form (files tests/reporters/testSummary.ts, tests/unit/testSummary.test.ts, vitest.config.ts; source b27d726a692fe16cb8f2a4a523467308472bdbdf on snapshot 5c1a734e)
open_assumptions: The 60 Hz clock uses Colyseus Room.setFixedTimestep, which replaces the deprecated setSimulationInterval that the decisions name. It is the same Colyseus facility.

Colyseus 0.18 answers matchmaking over HTTP, so join refusals use HTTP status codes: 426 protocol mismatch, 404 no match with that code, 409 match full, 400 malformed request. Each carries a readable message.
Movement axes outside [-1, 1] are rejected by the protocol, not clamped. The simulation also clamps its integer inputs defensively.

Input validation runs in the room's onMessage through packages/protocol, not through Colyseus's built-in validate() or defineInput. Colyseus disconnects the client on a failed validation, but the task says to drop such messages.

The room drops over-cap input (60 messages per second of match time, 128 bytes per message) and unknown message types. Colyseus's own hard limits above that disconnect the client: WebSocket frames over 4 KiB (ws maxPayload) and more than 240 messages a second.

The colyseus 0.18.8 meta package brings in uWebSockets.js as a GitHub git dependency (a non-optional peer of @colyseus/uwebsockets-transport), so npm ci needs github.com. Verified here with an empty cache and ssh disabled; it was fetched over https.

No package is pinned to a previous major. Pinned versions: typescript 7.0.2, vite 8.3.0, vitest 5.0.1, phaser 4.2.1, colyseus 0.18.8, @colyseus/schema 5.0.34, @colyseus/sdk 0.18.4, @playwright/test 1.63.0, zod 4.6.5, tsx 4.23.15, concurrently 10.0.5.
apps/web and packages/test-tools import only types from @pirate-sea-race/server/schema. They decode state through Colyseus reflection and share no runtime code with the server.

Workspace packages export a '@pirate-sea-race/source' condition that points at src/, used by tsc typechecks, Vite, Vitest and tsx. The Playwright webServer runs the server from source with tsx and serves a fresh vite build through vite preview, so it does not need a prior npm run build.
The map bounds are 0 to width×256−1 (and the same for height), so every position lies on a real tile.

findings.message: Private matches can be joined without their code. authorizeEntry (apps/server/src/MatchRoom.ts:44-50) treats any request whose options lack `code` as a create request and accepts it once createMatchOptionsSchema passes. Colyseus 0.18 exposes `join` and `joinOrCreate` over the HTTP matchmaker (@colyseus/core matchmaker/controller.mjs exposedMethods). For `join`/`joinOrCreate` with just {protocolVersion:1}, findOneRoomAvailable (MatchMaker.mjs:172-183) filters only on {locked:false,name:'match',private:false}, because getFilterOptions adds nothing without `code`. It therefore returns an arbitrary open private match and reserves a seat in it. Rooms are not marked private, and onJoin never checks the requested code against state.code. So any client can join a stranger's match without its code, bypassing the 'No match with that code' refusal. No integration test covers a codeless join. Fix: refuse `join`/`joinOrCreate` without a valid code (for example check options.code === this.state.code in onJoin for every non-creator, or narrow the exposed matchmaker methods to create and join and require a code for join), and add a regression test.
findings.requirement: One Colyseus room per match. Players join a private match by code. A private match holds 1 to 8 players and is marked custom (§2). A join whose protocol version differs from the server's is refused with a message the client shows.

findings.message: The full-match refusal in onAuth reads the listing before Colyseus reserves the seat. If two joins arrive while the match has seven players, the one that loses the race is refused by Colyseus's own 'no rooms found' error (MATCHMAKE_INVALID_CRITERIA). The client (apps/web/src/connection.ts:29) maps that error to 'No match with that code' instead of the full-match message. Capacity itself is still enforced by Colyseus locking.
findings.requirement: One Colyseus room per match. Players join a private match by code. A private match holds 1 to 8 players and is marked custom (§2). A join whose protocol version differs from the server's is refused with a message the client shows.

findings.message: InputGate uses an input's frame tag only for the 30-frame future-window check. An accepted input is held and applied from the next step no matter which frame it names (apps/server/src/inputGate.ts:39-51). This is acceptable without prediction, but the frame tag has no other effect, and that should be recorded as a known limitation before the combat spike relies on frame-accurate input.
findings.requirement: Clients send intent only: a frame-tagged input with a sequence number, buttons and bounded movement axes.

findings.message: If allocateCode fails 16 times, onCreate throws ServerError(400, 'Could not allocate a match code'), which Colyseus returns to the client as a create failure. This is only reachable with extreme numbers of live rooms, so it is a note rather than a defect.

# Decisions: skeleton

From the grill session of 2026-09-24 with the operator (question 1 in md-manager's session, questions 2–5 in the workflow-grill session).

## Decisions

- Scope: a walking skeleton. It covers the §17 layout and toolchain plus one thin end-to-end path, where browsers join a private match and see ships the server moves. There are no combat, islands or rubbings. A tooling-only scaffold and the §18 stage 1 combat spike were rejected.
- Numbers in `packages/simulation` are integers (fixed-point): every position, velocity and speed in the state is an integer, and the step function never calls `Math.sin`, `Math.cos`, `Math.sqrt` or other floating-point transcendental functions. Diagonal movement is normalised with an integer approximation or lookup table. Consequence: `hashState` is engine-independent, so the combat spike can run the same step in browsers without changing the state shape.
- The sea is a map grid laid out like coordinates: a bounded rectangle with the origin (0,0) at the top-left, x increasing right and y increasing down. It is made of tiles, each split into a fixed integer number of sub-units. Ships move continuously in sub-units, not tile by tile, and are clamped to the map bounds. Positions can be read as a tile plus an offset. Tile size, map size in tiles and ship speed are typed data in `packages/content`.
- State sync: `apps/server` holds a Colyseus Schema state that mirrors the plain simulation state after each world step, and the client decodes it with `@colyseus/sdk`. `packages/protocol` defines client→server messages, their validation and the protocol version, not the synced state shape. Consequence: delta patches and the patch rate come from Colyseus, and §16's per-player hidden information can later use Colyseus StateView.
- Use existing tooling rather than rebuilding it: when a maintained library or a framework feature already solves a problem, use it (for example Colyseus matchmaking, `filterBy`, Schema and the simulation interval; a schema library for protocol validation; Vitest projects; Playwright `webServer`). Every workspace keeps a conventional, consistent layout (`src/`, tests next to or under it, its own `package.json` and `tsconfig.json` extending `tsconfig.base.json`). Consequence: reviewers may flag hand-rolled replacements for standard tools.
- Player count: a private match holds 1 to 8 players and is marked custom. A ship spawns and can sail as soon as its player joins, with no lobby phase, ready check, start button or match timer. A ninth join is refused with a message the client shows. This intentionally differs from §2's "two to eight" for private tests; that minimum arrives with match phases.
- Private match codes: the landing page has a "Create match" button and a "Join" field. Create makes a room with a server-generated six-character code (uppercase letters and digits, for example `K7Q2MX`), shown in the HUD. Join accepts only an existing code (case-insensitive) and shows "No match with that code" otherwise. Rooms are found with Colyseus `filterBy(['code'])`.
- Scenario `join-private-match`: the browser creates a match from the landing page, and the HUD shows its code, the protocol version, one player and "connected". This satisfies the scenario's "enters a private match code". Scenario `two-ships-sync`: the first context creates the match, and the second reads the code from the first context's HUD and joins with it.

## Assumptions

- The pure packages may depend on plain TypeScript libraries (for example a schema validation library) as long as those libraries do not bring in Phaser, Colyseus, DOM APIs, timers, wall-clock time or `Math.random`. The purity unit test checks the packages' own source imports.
- The server runs the 60 Hz match clock with Colyseus's simulation interval, runs world logic (ship movement) on every third step, and patches clients at 20 Hz or less. The client interpolates between patches for drawing. The DOM readout of authoritative positions shows the latest decoded server values, not interpolated ones.
- Clients tag each input with their estimate of the server frame, based on the last patched frame. The server drops inputs whose sequence is not strictly greater than the last accepted one from that client, and inputs whose frame is more than a fixed window (at most 30 frames) ahead of its current frame. It caps message size and per-client message rate, and drops anything over the caps without crashing.
- Movement axes are integers or numbers in [-1, 1], and out-of-range values are rejected (the worker may choose clamping instead, but must test whichever it chooses). Buttons are a bit field. Only movement is used in this feature.
- Spawn positions come from a fixed list of eight spawn slots in `packages/content`, and the seeded generator in the match state assigns them. Two ships never share a slot.
- The protocol version is a single constant exported by `packages/protocol`. The client sends it in its join options, and the server refuses a mismatched version in `onAuth` or `onJoin` with a readable error that the client shows.
- When a client leaves, its ship is removed. There is no reconnection.
- Playwright's `webServer` entries start the server on 2593 and the web client on 5393 without depending on a prior `npm run build`: they either run the dev servers or build what they need themselves.
- The shared frame-budget table and rules presets live in `packages/content` as typed data with a validator. They are not used by the simulation yet.
- A package that the policy lets a worker pin to its previous major is recorded as an open assumption in the worker's result and in `docs/architecture.md`.

## Deferred

- Match phases from §2: lobby, ready check, the two-player minimum for private tests, departure protection, the match timer and results.
- Reconnection with expiring reconnect credentials, sessions and guest identity (§16).
- Per-player hidden information through Colyseus StateView (§16), and the content hash in the join check (§17).
- Client-side prediction and reconciliation, the network impairment harness and the replay runner in `packages/test-tools` (§15, §17), all left to the combat spike.
- Islands, tile-editor maps, combat, duels, rubbings, fruits, economy, accounts, the HTTP service, PostgreSQL, deployment and controllers.

concerns.message: filterBy(['code']) with a code generated on the server is fragile. Colyseus fills the filterBy fields of a room's listing from the client's create options, not from values set in onCreate. A code generated in onCreate is therefore not in the listing unless the room writes `this.listing.code` itself. Two more traps: a room marked with `setPrivate()` (the word 'private' invites it) is left out of `join()` queries, and a full room is locked and also left out.
concerns.consequence: Joining by code always fails with 'no rooms found' until the worker finds the listing detail. Even after that, a ninth player who joins a full room is told 'No match with that code' instead of a 'match is full' refusal, because matchmaking cannot tell a full room from an unknown code. The integration test or a reviewer will catch this late.

concerns.message: Package resolution when nothing is built yet. The verifier runs typecheck, unit and integration before build in a clean worktree, and dist/ is gitignored. The Playwright web servers must also start without a prior build. If a workspace's package.json `exports` or `main` points at dist/, checks pass in the worker's worktree, where dist/ is left over from earlier builds, and fail at the verifier. The server's build output also has to work at runtime: Node 24 type stripping does not handle workspace TypeScript imported without `.ts` extensions.
concerns.consequence: A green local run turns into a verifier failure and uses one of the three verification attempts. The fix then means rewiring package exports across all six workspaces.

concerns.message: The rule allowing the previous major for 'that one package' does not fit Colyseus. The server (`colyseus`/`@colyseus/core`), `@colyseus/schema` and the client SDK are versioned as a set. `@colyseus/sdk` is, as far as I know, the 0.17-era name; the 0.16 client was `colyseus.js`. Falling back to the previous version of only one of them does not work.
concerns.consequence: If 0.17 misbehaves on Node 24, the worker might pair a 0.16 server with the 0.17 SDK (handshake or schema decode failures), or report `blocked` even though the matched 0.16 set would work. The decision's wording ("decodes with @colyseus/sdk") would then also be wrong.

concerns.message: Schema decorators and class fields. With `@type()` decorators and `useDefineForClassFields` on (the default for ES2022+ targets, and what esbuild/oxc in Vitest and Vite follow), class field initialisers overwrite the accessors the decorators install. Mutations then stop producing patches, and no error is raised. Whether the TypeScript version the task calls current stable still supports legacy `experimentalDecorators` is a further risk.
concerns.consequence: Ship positions change on the server but never reach clients. The integration and two-ships-sync tests time out and give no clear cause, which can cost hours. The schema() or defineTypes helpers (no decorators) avoid the problem.

concerns.message: Purity is not enforced by what the plan names. Leaving out the DOM lib does not remove `setTimeout`, `performance` and similar globals when `@types/node` sits hoisted at the root: TypeScript picks up every `@types/*` package unless `types: []` is set. An import-only purity test also cannot catch `Math.random`, `Date.now` or timers, because those are globals, not imports.
concerns.consequence: The purity unit test passes while a pure package calls `Math.random` or `setTimeout`, so the determinism guarantee the combat spike depends on is not actually checked. The pure packages' tsconfig needs `types: []`, and the purity test needs a source scan for those identifiers.

concerns.message: Movement tests can be flaky because of spawn slots and map bounds. §2 describes 'outer-world' spawn slots, and ships are clamped to the map. If the seeded generator puts the first ship at an edge and the e2e test presses toward that edge, the position does not change. In the same way, a 'one-input change' in the determinism test can land on a clamped ship, or on a non-world step that is never read, and produce the same hash.
concerns.consequence: two-ships-sync, or the hash-difference unit test, fails intermittently depending on the match seed. That is flakiness the verifier rejects, and it is hard to reproduce. Spawn slots should sit further inside the map than a test moves a ship, and tests should move toward the map centre.

concerns.message: 'Both ships are drawn on the canvas' has no specified way to be observed. With WebGL, `toDataURL` and `getImageData` read back blank unless `preserveDrawingBuffer` is set. Headless Chromium on a VPS without a GPU may not provide WebGL at all.
concerns.consequence: The worker either weakens the check to the DOM readout, which a reviewer will flag as not proving rendering, or writes pixel checks that pass locally and fail under the verifier. A small test hook that exposes the scene's ship sprites, or the Canvas renderer in tests, avoids both.

concerns.message: Playwright webServer on the fixed ports 2593 and 5393 with `reuseExistingServer: true`. If the worker leaves a dev server running, a later run reuses that stale process instead of starting the code under test.
concerns.consequence: Browser checks pass or fail against old code. The worker's own report.json can then disagree with the verifier's result.

challenge.simpler_alternative: Make every workspace package source-only: `exports` points at `src/index.ts`. Typecheck with `tsc -b` or per-workspace `tsc --noEmit`, run Vitest and Vite dev straight from source, and have `apps/server`'s build bundle its workspace dependencies (esbuild or Vite SSR) into one runnable `dist/index.js`. This removes the question of whether dist/ exists, for every check and for the Playwright web servers. For match codes, if filterBy's listing and locked-room behaviour gets in the way, set `this.roomId = code` in onCreate and join with `joinById(code.toUpperCase())`. That gives distinct errors for an unknown code and a full room, with no matchmaking filter at all. This conflicts with decisions.md, so only use it if the filterBy spike fails.
challenge.cheap_experiment: A 20–30 minute spike in a scratch directory on Node 24, using the exact versions the worker plans to pin (colyseus, @colyseus/schema, @colyseus/sdk, TypeScript, Vitest). Write one Vitest file that boots a Colyseus server on port 0 with a room defined `.filterBy(['code'])`. The room generates a six-character code in onCreate and sets the listing field, and its state has one Schema map of ships with integer x and y fields, declared the way the worker intends (decorators or schema()). Client A calls `create`. Client B calls `join` with the code. The server changes a ship's x inside `setSimulationInterval`. Assert that B decodes the new x, that a wrong code and a ninth join are rejected with distinguishable messages, and that a mismatched `protocolVersion` in onAuth rejects with a readable error. If the version set, filterBy with a server-generated code, or Schema sync under Vitest's transform fails here, the pins or the code mechanism change before any real work starts.

# Task: game

## Goal

Turn the empty repository into the walking skeleton of the game in `docs/spec.md`: the §17 monorepo layout with a working TypeScript toolchain, and one thin end-to-end path through it. Browsers join a private match on the authoritative Colyseus server and sail placeholder ships. The shared fixed-step simulation moves each ship, and every browser in the match sees the result.

## Context

- Read `docs/spec.md` §14 (architecture), §15 (networking), §16 (data contracts and security) and §17 (repository layout) first. Everything else describes the game this skeleton will grow into; do not build it.
- The repository has only the spec, `CLAUDE.md` and `features/`. Node 24 and npm 11 are installed. Playwright's Chromium for `@playwright/test` 1.63.0 is already installed on this machine (the verifier shares `~/.cache/ms-playwright` read-only), so pin `@playwright/test` to exactly `1.63.0` and never run `playwright install`.
- The verifier runs `npm ci` in a clean worktree with an empty npm cache, then the policy's checks: `npm run typecheck`, `npm run test:unit`, `npm run test:integration`, `npm run build` and `npx --no-install playwright test --config=tests/e2e/playwright.config.ts`. Each must exist and pass from a clean checkout. Commit `package-lock.json`.

## Constraints

- npm workspaces: `apps/web`, `apps/server`, `packages/simulation`, `packages/protocol`, `packages/content` and `packages/test-tools`, as in §17. Add `assets/source`, `assets/exported` and `infra` as directories holding only a short README that says what will go there.
- Root files only at the paths the policy owns: `package.json`, `package-lock.json`, `tsconfig.json`, `tsconfig.base.json`, `vitest.config.ts`, `.gitignore`, `.npmrc`, `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `docs/architecture.md`. Everything else goes under `apps/`, `packages/`, `tests/`, `assets/`, `infra/` or `scripts/`. Never change `docs/spec.docx`, `docs/spec.md` or `features/`. In `CLAUDE.md`, change only the commands line and keep the "Workflow (operator notes)" section as it is.
- `packages/simulation`, `packages/protocol` and `packages/content` are pure: no Phaser, Colyseus, DOM, timers, wall-clock time or `Math.random`. Their tsconfig leaves the DOM library out, and a unit test fails if any of their source files imports one of these.
- The simulation follows §15: one 60 Hz match clock, with world logic every third step (20 Hz). State is plain serializable data. Randomness comes from a seeded generator kept in the state. `hashState(state)` returns a stable hash of the complete state.
- The server is the only writer of match state (§14, §16). Clients send intent only: a frame-tagged input with a sequence number, buttons and bounded movement axes. The server validates every message against `packages/protocol` and drops malformed, oversized or out-of-sequence ones without crashing. The client renders the server's state with interpolation. Client-side prediction and reconciliation belong to the combat spike.
- One Colyseus room per match. Players join a private match by code. A private match holds 1 to 8 players and is marked custom (§2). A join whose protocol version differs from the server's is refused with a message the client shows.
- Pin exact dependency versions: current stable TypeScript, Vite, Vitest, Phaser, `colyseus`, `@colyseus/sdk` and `@playwright/test` 1.63.0. If a current major version cannot work with the others, you may use the previous major of that one package. Record it as an open assumption.
- Fixed local ports: server 2593, web 5393 (the Playwright config starts both). Nothing else on this machine uses them.
- Placeholder art: coloured shapes drawn by Phaser. Do not add image or audio files.
- Out of scope: combat, duels, islands, rubbings, fruits, economy, accounts, the HTTP service, PostgreSQL, deployment, controllers and client prediction.

## Acceptance

- `npm ci` then each of the five policy checks passes from a clean checkout.
- Unit (`npm run test:unit`, Vitest):
  - determinism: the same initial state and input log give the same `hashState` after 600 steps, and a one-input change gives a different hash;
  - world logic advances only on every third step;
  - protocol validation accepts a valid input and rejects malformed, oversized and future-frame inputs;
  - a movement axis outside [-1, 1] is clamped or rejected;
  - the purity rule holds for the three pure packages;
  - `packages/content` exports the rules presets `slice` and `alpha` with §18's differences (two versus four rubbing types, 8 versus 12 rubbings, 4 versus 12 islands) and §8's baseline frame-budget table as typed data, with a validator that rejects impossible timings (non-positive startup or active frames, for example).
- Integration (`npm run test:integration`): starts the real server in-process on a free port. `packages/test-tools` provides a headless client, and two such clients join the same private code. Inputs from one move its ship on the server, and both clients observe the same authoritative position. A client with a different protocol version is refused. # Decisions: skeleton

From the grill session of 2026-09-24 with the operator (question 1 in md-manager's session, questions 2–5 in the workflow-grill session).

## Decisions

- Scope: a walking skeleton. It covers the §17 layout and toolchain plus one thin end-to-end path, where browsers join a private match and see ships the server moves. There are no combat, islands or rubbings. A tooling-only scaffold and the §18 stage 1 combat spike were rejected.
- Numbers in `packages/simulation` are integers (fixed-point): every position, velocity and speed in the state is an integer, and the step function never calls `Math.sin`, `Math.cos`, `Math.sqrt` or other floating-point transcendental functions. Diagonal movement is normalised with an integer approximation or lookup table. Consequence: `hashState` is engine-independent, so the combat spike can run the same step in browsers without changing the state shape.
- The sea is a map grid laid out like coordinates: a bounded rectangle with the origin (0,0) at the top-left, x increasing right and y increasing down. It is made of tiles, each split into a fixed integer number of sub-units. Ships move continuously in sub-units, not tile by tile, and are clamped to the map bounds. Positions can be read as a tile plus an offset. Tile size, map size in tiles and ship speed are typed data in `packages/content`.
- State sync: `apps/server` holds a Colyseus Schema state that mirrors the plain simulation state after each world step, and the client decodes it with `@colyseus/sdk`. `packages/protocol` defines client→server messages, their validation and the protocol version, not the synced state shape. Consequence: delta patches and the patch rate come from Colyseus, and §16's per-player hidden information can later use Colyseus StateView.
- Use existing tooling rather than rebuilding it: when a maintained library or a framework feature already solves a problem, use it (for example Colyseus matchmaking, `filterBy`, Schema and the simulation interval; a schema library for protocol validation; Vitest projects; Playwright `webServer`). Every workspace keeps a conventional, consistent layout (`src/`, tests next to or under it, its own `package.json` and `tsconfig.json` extending `tsconfig.base.json`). Consequence: reviewers may flag hand-rolled replacements for standard tools.
- Player count: a private match holds 1 to 8 players and is marked custom. A ship spawns and can sail as soon as its player joins, with no lobby phase, ready check, start button or match timer. A ninth join is refused with a message the client shows. This intentionally differs from §2's "two to eight" for private tests; that minimum arrives with match phases.
- Private match codes: the landing page has a "Create match" button and a "Join" field. Create makes a room with a server-generated six-character code (uppercase letters and digits, for example `K7Q2MX`), shown in the HUD. Join accepts only an existing code (case-insensitive) and shows "No match with that code" otherwise. Rooms are found with Colyseus `filterBy(['code'])`.
- Scenario `join-private-match`: the browser creates a match from the landing page, and the HUD shows its code, the protocol version, one player and "connected". This satisfies the scenario's "enters a private match code". Scenario `two-ships-sync`: the first context creates the match, and the second reads the code from the first context's HUD and joins with it.

## Assumptions

- The pure packages may depend on plain TypeScript libraries (for example a schema validation library) as long as those libraries do not bring in Phaser, Colyseus, DOM APIs, timers, wall-clock time or `Math.random`. The purity unit test checks the packages' own source imports.
- The server runs the 60 Hz match clock with Colyseus's simulation interval, runs world logic (ship movement) on every third step, and patches clients at 20 Hz or less. The client interpolates between patches for drawing. The DOM readout of authoritative positions shows the latest decoded server values, not interpolated ones.
- Clients tag each input with their estimate of the server frame, based on the last patched frame. The server drops inputs whose sequence is not strictly greater than the last accepted one from that client, and inputs whose frame is more than a fixed window (at most 30 frames) ahead of its current frame. It caps message size and per-client message rate, and drops anything over the caps without crashing.
- Movement axes are integers or numbers in [-1, 1], and out-of-range values are rejected (the worker may choose clamping instead, but must test whichever it chooses). Buttons are a bit field. Only movement is used in this feature.
- Spawn positions come from a fixed list of eight spawn slots in `packages/content`, and the seeded generator in the match state assigns them. Two ships never share a slot.
- The protocol version is a single constant exported by `packages/protocol`. The client sends it in its join options, and the server refuses a mismatched version in `onAuth` or `onJoin` with a readable error that the client shows.
- When a client leaves, its ship is removed. There is no reconnection.
- Playwright's `webServer` entries start the server on 2593 and the web client on 5393 without depending on a prior `npm run build`: they either run the dev servers or build what they need themselves.
- The shared frame-budget table and rules presets live in `packages/content` as typed data with a validator. They are not used by the simulation yet.
- A package that the policy lets a worker pin to its previous major is recorded as an open assumption in the worker's result and in `docs/architecture.md`.

## Deferred

- Match phases from §2: lobby, ready check, the two-player minimum for private tests, departure protection, the match timer and results.
- Reconnection with expiring reconnect credentials, sessions and guest identity (§16).
- Per-player hidden information through Colyseus StateView (§16), and the content hash in the join check (§17).
- Client-side prediction and reconciliation, the network impairment harness and the replay runner in `packages/test-tools` (§15, §17), all left to the combat spike.
- Islands, tile-editor maps, combat, duels, rubbings, fruits, economy, accounts, the HTTP service, PostgreSQL, deployment and controllers.

handoff.summary: Built the §17 walking skeleton as npm workspaces: apps/web (Phaser client with landing page, HUD, keyboard adapter, input sender, snapshot interpolation), apps/server (Colyseus MatchRoom: one room per private match, filterBy code, static onAuth refusing protocol mismatch/unknown code/full match, 60 Hz setFixedTimestep with world logic every third step, Schema mirror patched at 20 Hz, InputGate dropping malformed/oversized/stale/future-frame/over-rate input), packages/simulation (integer fixed-point state, seeded mulberry32 in state, spawn slots, hashState = FNV-1a 64 over canonical JSON), packages/protocol (version, zod join/input schemas, validation), packages/content (sea map, spawn slots, ship speed, slice/alpha presets, §8 frame budgets with validators), packages/test-tools (HeadlessClient on @colyseus/sdk). Added README.md, docs/architecture.md, the CLAUDE.md commands line, and READMEs for assets/source, assets/exported and infra. open_assumptions: The 60 Hz clock uses Colyseus Room.setFixedTimestep, which replaces the deprecated setSimulationInterval that the decisions name. It is the same Colyseus facility.

Colyseus 0.18 answers matchmaking over HTTP, so join refusals use HTTP status codes: 426 protocol mismatch, 404 no match with that code, 409 match full, 400 malformed request. Each carries a readable message.
Movement axes outside [-1, 1] are rejected by the protocol, not clamped. The simulation also clamps its integer inputs defensively.

Input validation runs in the room's onMessage through packages/protocol, not through Colyseus's built-in validate() or defineInput. Colyseus disconnects the client on a failed validation, but the task says to drop such messages.

The room drops over-cap input (60 messages per second of match time, 128 bytes per message) and unknown message types. Colyseus's own hard limits above that disconnect the client: WebSocket frames over 4 KiB (ws maxPayload) and more than 240 messages a second.

The colyseus 0.18.8 meta package brings in uWebSockets.js as a GitHub git dependency (a non-optional peer of @colyseus/uwebsockets-transport), so npm ci needs github.com. Verified here with an empty cache and ssh disabled; it was fetched over https.

No package is pinned to a previous major. Pinned versions: typescript 7.0.2, vite 8.3.0, vitest 5.0.1, phaser 4.2.1, colyseus 0.18.8, @colyseus/schema 5.0.34, @colyseus/sdk 0.18.4, @playwright/test 1.63.0, zod 4.6.5, tsx 4.23.15, concurrently 10.0.5.
apps/web and packages/test-tools import only types from @pirate-sea-race/server/schema. They decode state through Colyseus reflection and share no runtime code with the server.

Workspace packages export a '@pirate-sea-race/source' condition that points at src/, used by tsc typechecks, Vite, Vitest and tsx. The Playwright webServer runs the server from source with tsx and serves a fresh vite build through vite preview, so it does not need a prior npm run build.
The map bounds are 0 to width×256−1 (and the same for height), so every position lies on a real tile.
